We demonstrate that neural networks can overinterpret input data, and that this phenomenon can lead to high accuracy on popular image benchmarks even when the input is heavily occluded and humans cannot discern class-specific features.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that overinterpretation exists, it is a problem, but it is also a symptom of the training procedure.
we show that overinterpretation is a real phenomenon, and it can be mitigated to some degree.
overinterpretation is a form of model pathology, but it is a natural pathology of popular image classifiers, not a pathological behavior that can be exploited to fool a model.
The main takeaway from our work is that
high scoring models can be overfit to the statistical properties of a dataset, and that overinterpretation can serve as a useful proxy for this type of model pathology.
the high test set accuracy of modern CNNs can obscure subtle but troubling pathologies.
overinterpretation is a common phenomenon, but it is also a symptom of a deeper problem: the lack of human supervision in training.
